ABSTRACT
This study proposes a hybrid renewable energy system (HRES) that integrates photovoltaic panels (PVs), wind
turbines (WTs), and continuous green hydrogen production via reformers. To enhance system reliability and
efficiency, hybrid storage solutions, including hydrogen tanks and batteries, are incorporated. An integrated size
and design optimization algorithm (i-NSGA-II), based on the Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm-II
(NSGA-II), is proposed, combining the system design optimization with an advanced power management
strategy (PMS). The proposed approach is validated through comparison with multi-objective particle swarm
optimization (MOPSO). In the hydrogen storage scenario, the minimum annualized cost of system (ACS) solu-
tions achieved a 10% reduction in ACS, the minimum loss of power supply probability (LPSP) solutions showed a
78% decrease in LPSP, and the minimum percentage of energy waste (PEW) solutions resulted in an 83%
reduction in PEW compared to MOPSO. In the hybrid storage scenario, the results showed a 9% reduction in ACS
and an 85% decrease in LPSP for the corresponding objective functions compared to MOPSO. For both minimum
PEW solutions in the hybrid storage scenario, the PEW value was 0%, achieving 100% system efficiency. Sim-
ulations conducted in three regions demonstrated the system ’ s adaptability to varying climatic and regional
conditions. A comprehensive sensitivity analysis reveals the impacts of cost variations, storage types, and ca-
pacities on system performance, providing insights into the trade-offs involved in optimizing HRES.
1. Introduction
The depletion of fossil fuel reserves and their significant environ-
mental consequences have heightened the demand for sustainable en-
ergy alternatives. Solar and wind power have emerged as leading
candidates due to their availability and environmental benefits. [ 1 ].
However, it is well-known that when used alone, the unpredictable and
intermittent nature of these resources often fails to sufficiently meet the
cost and reliability expectations for providing energy to either a single
residence or larger-scale systems. To address this challenge and better
harness these renewable resources, hybrid energy systems have been
developed, incorporating them together along with power backup units
[ 2 – 4 ].
Building on the development of these hybrid energy systems, a
critical next step is to ensure their long-term viability through a
balanced optimization of various performance indicators. Studies have
shown that for these systems to be economically feasible, factors such as
system reliability, CO
2
emissions, and energy usage efficiency need to be
optimized, not just the system size. These findings underscore the
importance of employing advanced multi-objective optimization stra-
tegies like the Pareto optimization. The Pareto optimal solution
approach allows decision-makers to prioritize solution areas according
to their preferences [ 5 , 6 ]. The solution set obtained includes all optimal
solutions that cannot dominate each other, known as the Pareto Front, a
concept introduced by Vilfredo Pareto [ 7 , 8 ]. These solutions cannot be
improved in one objective without simultaneously worsening another,
thus they are not dominated by any other member within the population
[ 9 ].
Given its advantages, Pareto-based optimization has been widely
applied in HRES design. In this context, algorithms such as NSGA-II and
MOPSO are frequently used to balance multiple objectives. For instance,
Baghaee et al. proposed a novel method for minimizing the annual cost,
expected energy loss, and expected load loss, of a microgrid system
consisting of hydrogen storage, PV, wind, and fuel cells. This method is

another study on Pareto optimization, Ansari [11] focused on mini-

Additionally, a sensitivity analysis was performed, considering the im-
pacts of fuel and storage costs. Ma et al. [12] introduced a
Hypervolume-enhanced NSGA-III algorithm for the configuration of
HRES and evaluated its performance against other Pareto optimization
techniques like MOPSO. Their findings highlighted the hydrogen sub-
system’s role in improving system reliability and sustainability, along-
side the algorithm’s exceptional Pareto performance. Studies that
propose a Pareto-based multi-objective optimization method for HRESs
can also be examined in Refs. [13–17].
HRES composed entirely of renewable sources, along with diverse
storage technologies, are increasingly being adopted for zero-emission
and sustainable power solutions. In this context, the usage of
hydrogen in HRES, as both a renewable energy source and a storage tool,
is gradually increasing due to its clean, sustainable, and environmentally
friendly attributes [18].
In recent years, the production of hydrogen in HRES by splitting
water into hydrogen and oxygen atoms in electrolyzers using the sys-
tem’s excess energy has become widespread. A review of the literature
reveals that optimization studies on HRES using hydrogen obtained
through electrolysis as a storage medium are divided into two cate-
gories: systems entirely based on hydrogen storage and systems that also
utilize battery storage and/or other storage techniques. Focusing spe-
cifically on studies that utilize hydrogen storage alone, several optimi-
zation approaches have been proposed. Kalinci et al. [19] presented an
HRES model using hydrogen storage for Bozcaada Island in Türkiye.
Using the Hybrid Optimization Model for Electric Renewable (HOMER),
they determined the optimal system size providing minimum NPC and
cost of energy (COE) through scenarios comparing only wind turbines
and wind turbine/PV hybrid systems. They found that integrating PV
arrays with wind turbines significantly reduced the NPC, thereby
affecting the sizes of the hydrogen tank (HT) and other equipment, as
well as the COE. Samy et al. [20] developed the Flower Pollination Al-
gorithm (FPA) for size optimization of PV and fuel cell integrated energy
systems for remote and isolated regions in Egypt based on total annual
cost. MATLAB™ simulations demonstrated that FPA is faster and more
efficient compared to other optimization techniques. The optimal hybrid
system configuration resulted in a total net present value of $3,244,897
and an LCOE of $0.334/kWh, with LPSP constrained to 1.52%. In their
subsequent study, Samy et al. [21] present combinations of hybrid
systems: PV/FC, PV/WT/FC, and WT/FC. They compared the results
obtained from the FPA with those from the Shuffled Frog Leaping Al-
gorithm (SFLA) and the Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) techniques.
They demonstrated that the PV/wind/FC combination outperformed
others with an LCOE of $0.47/kWh. Ceylan and Devrim [22] designed
an HRES to provide electricity and heat to a greenhouse in S ¸ anlıurfa,
Türkiye, and optimized it using MATLAB/Simulink. In this system which
consists of PV, electrolyzers, and Proton Exchange Membrane Fuel Cells
(PEMFC), the heat generated by the PEMFCs was utilized to heat the
greenhouse through micro-cogeneration application. They calculated
the Levelized Cost of Energy (LCE) as $0.117/kWh for this system.
The integration of hydrogen storage with alternative energy storage
technologies, such as batteries, into HRES has garnered increasing
attention in recent years [23]. Numerous studies have explored the
single or multi-objective optimization of these systems. For instance,
Sharafi and ElMekkawy [24] developed a novel approach that combines
the ε -constraint method and PSO for the optimal design of a HRES
consisting of WTs, PV, DG, batteries, and hydrogen storage. Their model
simultaneously considers various renewable sources and storage de-
vices, aiming to minimize the total cost, unmet load, and fuel emissions
of the system. Altun and Kılıç [25] used a multi-objective optimization
method based on the Taguchi approach to minimize the levelized energy
cost and CO
2
emissions of grid-independent HRESs. They used battery
banks or hydrogen systems as energy backup units. Medghalchi and
Taylan [26] aimed to minimize energy costs across different scenarios
by integrating PV, WT with hydrogen or battery storage options. For this
purpose, they proposed a hybrid optimization system using PSO and
Genetic Algorithm. Their findings indicate that the PV-wind hybrid
system is the most effective with the lowest cost. Al-Quraan and
Athamnah [27] conducted size and energy management optimization
for a grid-independent HRES comprising WT and PV with battery and
hydrogen backup systems. They proposed a three-stage optimization
model consisting of nested loops to maximize system efficiency. They
achieved an average efficiency of 83.53% while minimizing the total
capital cost to $127,400 and the operating cost to $67. Another study
that combines battery and hydrogen backup systems was conducted by
Trapani et al. [28]. They utilized wind and solar energy as primary
sources in a fully reliable uninterrupted HRES and minimized the LCOE
using PSO. Song et al. [29] designed an off-grid HRES that utilizes solar
energy, hydrogen, and retired batteries to provide power and heat. To
optimize cost, improve reliability and minimize waste, they developed
an NSGA-II algorithm that integrates the Transient System Simulation
Program (TRNSYS) and MATLAB. Bade et al. [30] conducted the optimal
design of a HRES integrating WTs, PV systems, biomass, battery, and
hydrogen storage for a residential load, while considering technical,
economic, environmental, and social performance indicators. They
employed the hybrid genetic algorithm-particle swarm optimization
(GAPSO) algorithm as a multi-objective optimization approach. The
results of their study demonstrated that GAPSO achieved a
cost-effectiveness improvement of 2.17% compared to GA and 0.01%
compared to PSO.
In addition to integrating hydrogen and battery storage, studies
incorporating various alternative storage techniques into HRES have
also been conducted. In their research, Bryan et al. [31] devised an HRES
incorporating thermal and hydrogen storage alongside solar, wind, and
nuclear energy to fulfill all of Texas’s electricity requirements. Even
though the Levelized Cost of Energy (LCOE) obtained through their
proposed optimization algorithm surpasses that of the existing system,
they envisaged a system capable of generating carbon-free and green
hydrogen. Guo and Niu [32] developed an optimization approach that
integrates both single and multi-objective optimization for standalone
HRESs integrated with solar and wind energy, batteries, a hydrogen
energy storage system, and a thermal energy storage system. In the first
stage, LCOE and LPSP were evaluated as objective functions within the
multi-objective optimization framework. In the second stage, the
optimal LPSP values obtained were used as constraints, and the LCOE
was further optimized. The results demonstrated that lower LCOE values
were achieved compared to those obtained through multi-objective
optimization alone, while maintaining the same LPSP values. Jafarian
et al. [33] conducted a study using TRNSYS simulation, response surface
methodology, and life cycle assessment to highlight the trade-offs in
multi-objective optimization for energy storage capacity, renewable
fraction, and storage types. They assessed the impact of different energy
storage types, such as latent energy storage, hydrogen storage, and
battery storage, on optimal design. In another study, Li et al. [34] pro-
posed a collaborative framework between integrated energy systems
and hydrogen-natural gas energy storage system to enhance sustain-
ability and cost optimization. By employing a MOPSO method, the study
introduces advanced strategies for improving energy cooperation and
reducing costs. The results demonstrate significant profitability gains
and environmental advantages through better resource management.
Another method of obtaining hydrogen is the reforming of biogas
derived from biomass. Biogas produced in anaerobic digesters designed

HRESs are rare in literature. Hakimi and Tafreshi [38] used a fuel cell
powered by hydrogen obtained from a reformer, along with WTs and a
HT for storing excess energy, in an off-grid HRES. They utilized the PSO
algorithm for the system’s size optimization. Tezer and Yaman [9]
developed an NSGA–II–based algorithm for off-grid HRESs that includes
ACS and LPSP minimization. Their algorithm, which considers the LPSP
value and waste energy ratio as constraints, presents a PMS that maxi-

introduced an innovative design that incorporates hydrogen as an
uninterruptible power supply into the hybrid system optimization.
HassanzadehFard et al. [39] utilized two sources, methane produced
from wastes and purchased natural gas, for hydrogen production via a
reformer in a WT-PV-BESS-FC (reformer-fed) hybrid system. The mini-
mum NPC value of the system was calculated under a specific LPSP
constraint, where the reformer was not included in the size
optimization.
In the reviewed and accessible literature, it is observed that
hydrogen production in HRESs is often carried out using an electrolyzer
to store excess energy. System elements that produce hydrogen from
biomass, such as reformers, appear to be rarely used and are not
included in size optimization. Although many systems integrate
hydrogen and battery storage, such an integration has not been found in
the absence of an electrolyzer.

posed system, a comparison is made with the systems in the literature.

The main objective of this study is to address the limitations iden-
tified in the literature regarding hydrogen production and storage by
integrating uninterrupted hydrogen production from biomass sources
via a reformer and its storage into HRES, and optimizing system cost,
reliability, and efficiency with an innovative PMS. To achieve this, the i-
NSGA-II algorithm was developed for the sizing and optimization of
system components, and system performance was evaluated under
different climatic conditions.
Key differences and contributions of the proposed approach
compared to previous research.
⁃ Unlike many studies that focus solely on hydrogen storage using
electrolyzers, this research incorporates continuous hydrogen pro-
duction through reformers, ensuring an uninterrupted hydrogen
supply and enhancing system reliability and efficiency.
⁃ Two distinct energy storage strategies are proposed: Scenario 1 uti-
lizes two-source hydrogen storage, while Scenario 2 integrates
hybrid battery and hydrogen storage, providing alternative solutions
to optimize energy storage and reliability under varying conditions.
⁃ The PMS optimizes energy flows by efficiently utilizing hydrogen
and battery storage across different climatic conditions in Çes ¸ me,
Çanakkale, and Kahramanmaras ¸ , showcasing trade-offs between
cost, reliability, and efficiency.
⁃ A comprehensive system design optimization framework is intro-
duced, which not only integrates hydrogen production and hybrid
storage systems but also optimizes their sizes and configurations
based on specific conditions and interactions. This flexible approach
ensures a more tailored and efficient system design, enhancing the
practical applicability and flexibility of HRES configurations.
⁃ The study employs i-NSGA-II and validates its performance through a
comparison with the MOPSO, simultaneously optimizing cost, reli-
ability, and efficiency.
⁃ A comprehensive sensitivity analysis evaluates the effects of cost
variations, storage types, and capacities on system performance,
highlighting key factors that influence feasibility and providing in-
sights into the trade-offs in optimizing HRES.

below its minimum capacity. If there is still insufficient energy, it will be
provided by the fuel cell using hydrogen stored in HT, which is gener-

4.3. System design optimization
The proposed system design optimization approach differs from the
size optimization approach found in the literature because it determines
whether a component will be included in the system and, if included
what its type (size) and quantity will be. Therefore, the existence of an
element is denoted by two distinct structures, each representing its size
and number, with the total size being the product of these two. Addi-
tionally, this approach includes the necessary steps to design a system
where hydrogen can be present not only as an energy backup but also as
a direct energy source.
In Scenario 1, to ensure uninterrupted hydrogen production, if the
system includes a fuel cell, it is arranged to have a reformer of a size that
can meet the minimum hydrogen consumption and not exceed the
maximum hydrogen consumption of the fuel cell. Furthermore, to store
excess hydrogen, a HT is ensured to be included in the system alongside
the fuel cell in this case. Similarly, if an electrolyzer is present in the

cell-HT pair it will work with. The system is designed to ensure the
integrity of fuel cell-electrolyzer-HT or Reformer-fuel cell-HT energy
systems in a randomly generated initial population.
In Scenario 2, instead of an electrolyzer, a battery is included in the
system to store excess energy from PVs and WTs. In this case, the system
includes both a battery and hydrogen storage, ensuring energy balance.

4.4. Power management strategy (PMS)
The PMS regulates energy exchanges among the hybrid system
components to optimize system configuration by minimizing ACS, LPSP,
and PEW. This study utilizes hydrogen both as an uninterrupted power
source and for excess energy storage. The developed PMS ensures
effective energy flow between renewable energy sources and improves
both system reliability and efficiency by employing various energy
storage options tailored to each scenario.
In Scenario 1, the system utilizes hydrogen storage as the primary
solution for managing energy flow. Unlike conventional hydrogen
storage systems in the literature, this scenario incorporates an enhanced
PMS featuring hydrogen sourced from two different pathways. Excess
electricity generated by PVs and WTs is directed to the electrolyzer,
where it is converted into hydrogen. Additionally, when PV and WTs
generation meets or exceeds the load demand, surplus hydrogen pro-
duced by the reformer is also stored in HTs. During periods of insuffi-
cient renewable energy production, the stored hydrogen is utilized by
fuel cells to supply power, ensuring an uninterrupted energy flow. This
dual utilization of the electrolyzer and reformer for hydrogen produc-
tion, combined with efficient storage in HTs, significantly improves the
system ’ s reliability and operational flexibility.
With Scenario 2, a hybrid storage system has been aimed at
achieving the same objectives, where excess hydrogen from only the
reformer is stored in HTs and batteries are used for excess energy from
PVs and WTs. This hybrid approach aims to diversify storage options,
thereby improving the system ’ s overall flexibility and efficiency. Bat-
teries handle short-term fluctuations in renewable energy production,
whereas hydrogen storage addresses long-term energy needs. Fig. 5
presents a flowchart summarizing the working principle of the PMS for
Scenario 2, which includes hydrogen and battery storage. For Scenario 1
PMS, detailed explanations and a summary flow diagram can be
examined from the author ’ s previous work [ 9 ].

7. Conclusion
This study presents the optimization and analysis of a HRES inte-
grating PVs, WTs, and continuous green hydrogen production via re-
formers. The system incorporates hybrid storage solutions (HTs and
batteries) to enhance reliability and efficiency. The proposed system was
optimized using the i-NSGA-II algorithm, integrated with an advanced
PMS, and its effectiveness was validated through a comparative analysis
with MOPSO, confirming its superior performance. The key findings are
as follows.
➢ The Pareto optimal solutions for hydrogen storage and hybrid stor-
age scenarios in Çanakkale, Çes ¸ me, and Kahramanmaras ¸ were
compared. Scenario 2 outperformed Scenario 1 in terms of minimum
LPSP and PEW, whereas no significant difference was observed for
minimum ACS. Across all locations, the lowest LPSP solutions
exhibited a reduction in LPSP values ranging between 74% and 85%,
while a 100% reduction was achieved in the minimum PEW solu-
tions. Regarding minimum ACS solutions, in Kahramanmaras ¸ , Sce-
nario 1 provided only a slight advantage of 4% (from 5614.62 kWh
to 5821.96 kWh).
➢ In all three locations, the results indicate that prioritizing one
objective function requires compromising on others. Alternatively, a
solution that balances all three objectives can be selected from the
Pareto front. These findings emphasize that, in multi-objective
optimization problems, the selection among conflicting objective
functions depends on the preferences of decision-makers.
➢ The analyses conducted for three different cities have shown that the
optimal configuration of HRES is highly influenced by regional
conditions.
➢ The impacts of both regional and seasonal variations, as well as
storage options, on system performance have been demonstrated
through simulation results. The corresponding graphs show that the
total energy output from all system components, including fuel cells
and/or batteries, dynamically adapts to fluctuations in the load
profile curve. These results confirm the superior performance of the
developed PMS in ensuring secure and efficient system operations.
➢ Sensitivity analyses conducted to measure the impact of system
components on ACS revealed that ACS is more sensitive to changes in
the total costs of HT and fuel cell in Scenario 1, while in Scenario 2, it
is more sensitive to changes in battery and fuel cell costs.
➢ The analysis of the impact of storage systems on the objective
functions revealed that, in both scenarios, increasing the capacities
of the existing storage systems raises ACS values while significantly
enhancing system reliability and efficiency.
➢ The sensitivity analyses conducted separately for HT and battery in
hybrid storage revealed that HT has a greater impact on system
reliability, while the battery plays a more significant role in
enhancing system efficiency.
➢ The sensitivity analysis revealed that variations in costs, storage
types, and capacities significantly impact overall system
performance.
➢ Additionally, HRES optimization was performed using MOPSO under
the same conditions to validate the effectiveness of the proposed i-
NSGA-II. The results confirmed the superior performance of i-NSGA-
II, as it achieved better outcomes across all objective functions.
The results demonstrate that the proposed approach provides a
robust and flexible framework for optimizing HRES with green hydrogen
production and advanced storage solutions, paving the way for future
sustainable energy applications.
